highlights: Gas diplomacy balances Europe and Russia
State control remains strong over hydrocarbons

frictionVectors.title: European gas leverage
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian pipeline and LNG supplies, while Algeria relies on export revenue and European technology. Pricing, production capacity, and migration disputes periodically strain ties.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign energy participation
frictionVectors.details: International partners are returning under more favorable investment terms, but Algiers remains cautious about ceding operational or strategic control over upstream assets.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil output, foreign operators, and exposure to global price cycles constrain fiscal sovereignty. Debt servicing and production-sharing arrangements continue to channel significant value abroad.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, European partners, and China are competing for influence around the rail route linking Atlantic ports to critical-mineral regions. Infrastructure financing could improve diversification while creating new strategic dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou is expanding its role as a corridor hub, but trade and infrastructure remain exposed to foreign financiers, regional political shifts, and competition from neighboring ports.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity near the northern borders threatens transport routes, agricultural zones, and mining prospects. External security assistance is useful but increases reliance on outside partners.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market exposure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains strong institutional control and a comparatively balanced relationship with major diamond firms, but weak global demand can reduce fiscal space and bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: New minerals and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: Copper, nickel, and battery-mineral development may attract outside investors faster than domestic processing capacity can mature. The central challenge is securing local value addition without deterring capital.

highlights: Junta asserts control over gold resources

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater state participation and tighter oversight of industrial mining, but technical, financial, and marketing dependencies on foreign firms remain substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgent control and external realignment
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence disrupts mining zones, transport corridors, and agricultural production while weakening effective state control. The shift away from Western security partners toward Russia-linked assistance carries sovereignty and accountability risks.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Dependence and External Capital
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking to expand nickel and rare-earth production, but financing, technology, and export infrastructure remain heavily dependent on foreign partners. Weak bargaining power could limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Border and Security Friction
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed-group support and border security continue to disrupt regional commerce and constrain Burundi's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Ports and Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's ports, digital networks, and maritime-security capacity rely substantially on European, Chinese, and other external investment. This creates leverage risks around strategic Atlantic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on foreign tourism, remittances, and concessional finance leaves the economy exposed to external shocks despite strong institutions and relatively effective regulatory control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Resource Chains
frictionVectors.details: Oil, timber, mining, and major infrastructure projects depend heavily on foreign firms and lenders, while opaque contracts and limited processing capacity reduce domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Far-North Conflicts
frictionVectors.details: Insurgencies in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside Boko Haram-related violence in the Far North, weaken state control over transport corridors and resource regions.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-for-Access Model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel provide regime protection and combat support, while allegations of preferential access to gold and diamond networks raise concerns over sovereignty and accountability.

frictionVectors.title: Armed Groups and Border Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Weak state presence outside major urban areas allows armed groups and cross-border networks to influence mining, cattle, and trade routes, limiting national control over resources.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Dependence and Contractual Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenue remains central to public finance, leaving Chad vulnerable to price shocks and dependent on foreign operators, traders, and infrastructure providers for production and export.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: The reduced French military role and growing engagement by Gulf, Russian, and other external actors are reshaping security partnerships around the presidency, border control, and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and budget support remain heavily reliant on Gulf, French, and multilateral partners, limiting policy autonomy. Debt and project-finance constraints narrow the government's room to negotiate.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime sovereignty gap
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago's limited naval and coast-guard capacity leaves fisheries, maritime borders, and port approaches vulnerable to outside commercial and security interests.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt supply chains remain shaped by foreign firms, traders, and competing Chinese, Western, and Gulf interests. Kinshasa is seeking greater processing and revenue control, but governance and enforcement remain uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Regional proxy conflict
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in North and South Kivu continues to expose the limits of state sovereignty, with armed groups, regional actors, and illicit mineral networks intersecting. External mediation and security assistance have not yet produced durable control.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains the principal source of fiscal power, leaving national resource security exposed to price volatility and foreign-operated production arrangements. Local value addition and economic diversification remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-access bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign partners remain important in roads, ports, and energy projects, creating financing and sovereignty trade-offs. Debt exposure and opaque contracting can reduce public oversight of strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign ownership of strategic value chains
frictionVectors.details: Cocoa, energy, ports, and telecommunications remain closely linked to foreign capital and multinational firms. Abidjan is improving regulation and processing capacity, but domestic capture of value is still incomplete.

frictionVectors.title: Northern border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from the Sahel continues to pressure border communities and security spending. Expanded regional cooperation and investment in northern infrastructure are strengthening resilience but have not removed the risk.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military concentration
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military presences provide revenue and deterrence but constrain strategic autonomy and make Djibouti a node in wider-power rivalry. The government balances these relationships to preserve its bargaining leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's logistics economy depends on external trade, foreign operators, and infrastructure financing, particularly links serving Ethiopia. Debt burdens and contested port arrangements create persistent sovereignty and revenue risks.

frictionVectors.title: External financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt, foreign-exchange shortages, and reliance on IMF and Gulf-backed capital constrain Cairo's policy autonomy. Strategic assets and major development projects remain exposed to foreign ownership or management.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea shipping disruption
frictionVectors.details: Regional attacks and instability have reduced Suez Canal traffic and revenues, weakening a central pillar of Egypt's sovereign income and maritime influence.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon depletion
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields and limited diversification leave the state dependent on declining oil and gas revenues. Foreign energy firms retain significant technical and capital leverage over remaining production.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked construction and lending have expanded national infrastructure while increasing exposure to opaque repayment terms and external commercial influence.

frictionVectors.title: Ethiopia port ambitions
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopian efforts to secure Red Sea access keep Eritrea central to regional security calculations and raise the risk of coercive diplomacy or renewed confrontation.

frictionVectors.title: External military competition
frictionVectors.details: Red Sea naval activity and Gulf rivalries increase foreign interest in Eritrean ports, potentially expanding Asmara's bargaining power but also its exposure to outside pressure.

frictionVectors.title: South African dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade corridors, electricity, finance, and regional market access remain heavily dependent on South Africa, limiting Eswatini's strategic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, timber, and coal exports are exposed to foreign buyers, climate stress, and shifting regional trade rules, leaving limited domestic control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam has increased Addis Ababa's control over national electricity and water infrastructure while sustaining acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, foreign-exchange shortages, and reliance on external lenders constrain infrastructure policy. Internal conflict and insecurity further threaten transport, energy, and mining projects.

highlights: Junta-led transition seeks tighter control of oil and mining
France’s legacy influence is being recalibrated

frictionVectors.title: Resource Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are pursuing greater state participation and local value creation in oil, manganese, and iron projects. The challenge is attracting investment without weakening transparency or fiscal discipline.

frictionVectors.title: External Realignment
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is diversifying diplomatic and commercial ties beyond France toward Gulf, Chinese, and regional partners. This broadens options but may increase opaque contracting risks.

highlights: Small-state sovereignty remains tied to Senegalese security support
Tourism and coastal resources face external commercial pressure

frictionVectors.title: Senegambia Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional security, trade routes, and energy connectivity. This improves resilience but limits strategic autonomy during bilateral disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore and Fisheries Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and prospective offshore energy interests remain sensitive sovereignty issues. Weak enforcement capacity leaves coastal resources vulnerable to leakage.

highlights: Debt restructuring is constraining strategic policy space
Gold, lithium, and bauxite are central to a resource-nationalist agenda

frictionVectors.title: Mining Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is pressing for local processing and stronger state participation while confronting entrenched foreign mining interests and illegal mining. Environmental damage and revenue leakage remain major sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and external creditors constrain public investment choices. Chinese and Western financing competition is increasingly tied to infrastructure, minerals, and energy access.

highlights: Bauxite dominance is expanding toward Simandou-led iron ore power
Military rule centralizes resource decisions and limits accountability

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Corridor
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron ore project could transform state revenues and transport infrastructure, but its financing, ownership, and export logistics create major leverage for foreign partners. Local-content and environmental safeguards remain contested.

frictionVectors.title: Junta Governance
frictionVectors.details: Concentrated executive control enables rapid mining deals but reduces parliamentary and public oversight. Contract uncertainty and sanctions risk could complicate the country’s bargaining position.

highlights: Cashew dependence leaves the economy exposed to external buyers
Political instability weakens control of ports and maritime resources

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Value Chain
frictionVectors.details: Foreign traders and processors capture much of the value from Guinea-Bissau’s dominant export. Limited storage, processing, and financing capacity keeps producers vulnerable to price shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Security
frictionVectors.details: Bissau’s port and offshore waters attract competing foreign commercial and security interests amid weak institutions. The country remains vulnerable to illicit trafficking and opaque infrastructure agreements.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-financed infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kenya’s dependence on external financing for rail, ports, and energy infrastructure gives creditors and contractors significant influence over national development priorities. Debt-service pressures are narrowing Nairobi’s room to renegotiate major projects.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu corridor and coastal security
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu Port–South Sudan–Ethiopia corridor remains strategically important but faces insecurity, uneven regional development, and competition over control of logistics routes.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho’s water exports provide vital revenue, but the country remains heavily dependent on South Africa for financing, markets, and downstream infrastructure. Cost overruns and project delays could further weaken Lesotho’s bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mineral assets
frictionVectors.details: Diamond and other mineral operations rely substantially on foreign capital and technical capacity, limiting domestic value capture and exposing the economy to external commodity cycles.

highlights: Port and rail corridors invite competition

frictionVectors.title: Mining concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and emerging critical-mineral projects are structured around foreign operators and concession finance. Weak domestic processing capacity leaves Liberia vulnerable to revenue leakage and limited local value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Buchanan logistics corridor
frictionVectors.details: Control of ports, rail links, and export infrastructure is increasingly important as mining investment expands. Liberia must balance foreign operators’ infrastructure needs with public oversight and equitable access.

frictionVectors.title: Rival control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and security authorities continue to contest access to fields, export terminals, and revenue flows. Disruptions remain a persistent tool of bargaining, weakening the national oil sector’s unified sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: External military and energy influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign governments and contractors retain influence through security partnerships, arms networks, and energy interests. This complicates efforts to consolidate a single national command over ports, pipelines, and production assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mining value chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, graphite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented infrastructure. Madagascar captures employment and royalties but retains limited control over processing and pricing.

frictionVectors.title: Mining infrastructure and land conflict
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mines and associated roads, ports, and power systems can intensify disputes over land, water, and community compensation. Weak state capacity makes environmental enforcement and benefit-sharing difficult.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital and processing capacity remain essential to developing Malawi's uranium, rare-earth and niobium prospects. Limited domestic infrastructure weakens bargaining power over future projects.

frictionVectors.title: IMF-LED FISCAL PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and external financing conditions narrow the government's room to subsidize energy, transport and food systems. Public frustration could complicate reforms demanded by creditors.

highlights: Junta asserts control over gold resources

frictionVectors.title: MINING NATIONALISM
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking a larger state share and tighter oversight of gold mining, unsettling established foreign operators. Production and investment remain vulnerable to regulatory disputes and insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY FOOTPRINT
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security personnel and equipment is reshaping Mali's external alignment while increasing friction with Western partners. Armed-group violence continues to threaten roads, mines and power infrastructure.

highlights: Gas exports begin reshaping the economy

frictionVectors.title: GAS PROJECT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas development offers new state revenue but leaves Mauritania dependent on foreign operators, maritime infrastructure and cross-border coordination with Senegal.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND CORRIDOR BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports remain exposed to rail and port capacity constraints, while proposed green-hydrogen projects require large external capital commitments. Local value addition remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS AND MARITIME SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos settlement and management of maritime space remain strategically sensitive because of the Diego Garcia military facility. Mauritius must balance sovereignty claims with security ties involving the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE FINANCE SCRUTINY
frictionVectors.details: International tax and anti-money-laundering standards continue to pressure Mauritius's financial-services model. Compliance upgrades protect market access but reduce some policy flexibility.

highlights: Industrial policy deepens domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates, fisheries and infrastructure in Western Sahara remain central to Morocco's sovereignty strategy and a recurring source of legal and diplomatic friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front and European actors.

frictionVectors.title: GREEN-INDUSTRY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is attracting European, Gulf and Asian capital into batteries, renewables, ports and green hydrogen. External technology and financing remain important, creating exposure to shifting trade rules and investor leverage.

highlights: LNG revival remains hostage to Cabo Delgado security
Gas wealth is still largely externally financed

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence continues to constrain state control in the gas-producing north and threatens the restart and security of major LNG projects.

frictionVectors.title: LNG consortium leverage
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and lenders retain decisive influence over project timing, financing, and revenue structures, limiting near-term national bargaining power.

highlights: Oil and green-hydrogen deals test local value capture

frictionVectors.title: External control of new energy assets
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and financiers dominate the capital-intensive oil, hydrogen, uranium, and rare-earth pipeline, creating risks that Namibia exports resources without enough domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Walvis Bay is becoming more strategically important, but export diversification remains vulnerable to foreign shipping, infrastructure, and regional logistics partners.

highlights: Junta is renegotiating uranium and energy access
Security partnerships are shifting toward Russia and regional allies

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and mining sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is seeking greater control over uranium and other mineral concessions, producing sharp friction with established foreign operators and Western governments.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent attacks and political disputes affecting export routes, including the oil corridor to Benin, constrain revenue and expose Niger to infrastructure leverage from neighbors and external partners.

highlights: Domestic refining is expanding strategic autonomy
Oil theft and grid weakness still erode sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector leakage
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, pipeline vandalism, and opaque contracting continue to reduce public capture of hydrocarbons while leaving production and infrastructure vulnerable to private and external interests.

frictionVectors.title: Power and transport dependence
frictionVectors.details: Weak electricity and logistics networks limit industrial control despite major domestic investments, while Chinese, Gulf, and Western financiers compete for infrastructure influence.

highlights: Regional security policy drives external pressure

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-mineral allegations
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role in regional mineral supply chains remains contested amid allegations that trade routes benefit from conflict-linked resources originating in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo security entanglement
frictionVectors.details: Support for or alignment with forces operating in eastern Congo generates diplomatic, sanctions, and aid-related pressure that can constrain Kigali's economic and security choices.

highlights: Gulf of Guinea security cooperation expands

frictionVectors.title: Unproven Offshore Petroleum
frictionVectors.details: Exploration interest has not yet produced commercially confirmed reserves, leaving São Tomé and Príncipe vulnerable to unfavorable future contracts and revenue expectations.

frictionVectors.title: External Maritime Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies on foreign partners and regional mechanisms for maritime surveillance, fisheries protection, and port security in the Gulf of Guinea.

highlights: Gas and oil production reshapes fiscal sovereignty
Strategic balancing between Europe, Gulf states, and China

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Led Hydrocarbon Development
frictionVectors.details: New offshore gas and oil projects offer major revenue potential but remain dependent on foreign operators, imported technology, and long-term production-sharing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large transport and energy projects financed by external lenders can improve national capacity while narrowing fiscal room and increasing bargaining pressure from creditors.

highlights: Blue economy remains the core sovereign asset
Indian Ocean partnerships diversify security ties

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Maritime Capacity
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on external partners for maritime surveillance, patrol assets, and regional security despite its strategic location and extensive exclusive economic zone.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Fisheries Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on tourism and fisheries leaves the economy exposed to foreign demand, climate shocks, and external access arrangements affecting marine resources.

highlights: Mining revival tests local value capture

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Revenue and Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mining projects generate exports but remain dominated by foreign capital, creating persistent disputes over royalties, jobs, land, and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese-Backed Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed and -constructed infrastructure expands connectivity but can increase dependence on external contractors, imported inputs, and opaque commercial terms.

highlights: Ports and offshore hydrocarbons drive strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: Competing Port and Security Patrons
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, and other external actors compete for influence over ports, security arrangements, and logistics corridors, often bypassing or challenging federal cohesion.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Resource Governance
frictionVectors.details: Oil and gas licensing remains politically sensitive because weak institutions, maritime disputes, and limited enforcement capacity make future resource control vulnerable to foreign operators and elite capture.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND LOGISTICS BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability, rail congestion and port inefficiency continue to constrain mining exports and industrial sovereignty. Private investment and state reforms are improving capacity unevenly.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL CRITICAL-MINERALS PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The United States, European states and China are competing for access to platinum-group metals, manganese and other minerals. Pretoria retains formal control but faces pressure to align supply chains with external strategic blocs.

frictionVectors.title: OIL-PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on Sudanese export infrastructure, exposing its main revenue source to Sudan's war and pipeline disruption. Foreign operators and neighboring transit arrangements limit Juba's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: ELITE AND REGIONAL RESOURCE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation, armed groups and patronage networks obstruct transparent control of oil and land assets. Uganda, Sudan and other external actors retain influence through security and commercial ties.

highlights: Gold and ports attract external competition

frictionVectors.title: WAR ECONOMY AND GOLD SMUGGLING
frictionVectors.details: The SAF-RSF conflict has divided control of mines, trade corridors and revenue institutions. Gold flows and private security networks provide channels for foreign influence while weakening national resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA INFRASTRUCTURE CONTEST
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and associated military and logistics access are strategically contested by regional and global powers. War damage and competing external partnerships reduce Khartoum's ability to manage infrastructure on sovereign terms.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAILWAY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Standard Gauge Railway and port expansion strengthen Tanzania's regional position but rely on substantial foreign finance, contractors and technology. Dar es Salaam is balancing Chinese, Gulf, European and Indian interests.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL-MINERALS BARGAINING
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater local processing and state participation in gold, nickel and graphite projects. Negotiations with multinational investors remain a recurring test of fiscal sovereignty and environmental control.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hub

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is central to trade with landlocked Sahel markets and attracts sustained foreign commercial and infrastructure involvement. Dependence on external capital and shipping networks limits full national control of the logistics chain.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL JIHADIST SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Insecurity near the Burkina Faso border threatens roads, agricultural zones and northern mining activity. Togo is strengthening regional security cooperation while managing pressure from neighboring conflict zones and outside security partners.

highlights: Phosphate and energy security under pressure

frictionVectors.title: European Union Economic Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia relies heavily on European trade, tourism, financial support, and migration cooperation. Disputes over migration enforcement and democratic governance give Brussels significant negotiating influence.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic production and dependence on imported gas constrain Tunisia's economic sovereignty. Phosphate-sector disruptions further weaken export earnings and fiscal resilience.

frictionVectors.title: East African Crude Oil Pipeline
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania pipeline promises export revenue but locks strategic oil transport into foreign financing, operators, and regional infrastructure dependencies. Environmental opposition and Western scrutiny continue to raise political costs.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and External Capital
frictionVectors.details: Uganda is seeking investment in gold, copper, and rare-earth prospects while oversight capacity remains uneven. Foreign firms and regional trading networks can capture substantial value before revenues reach the state.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Ownership and Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using competition among Chinese, Gulf, Western, and regional investors to renegotiate mining terms. However, foreign ownership, concentration of smelting capacity, and commodity-price exposure still limit sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Power Supply Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortages threaten copper production and industrial reliability. Emergency imports and potential external financing for new generation increase infrastructure dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe has restricted exports of some unprocessed lithium and seeks domestic beneficiation, but Chinese firms remain central to capital, processing, and market access. Limited financing and technology constrain the state's ability to capture more value.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, restricted access to Western finance, and sanctions-linked compliance risks push Harare toward alternative lenders and investors. This narrows bargaining options and increases reliance on politically aligned external partners.
